newsitem.title: USA: American Exploration sees '97 production up.
newsitem.headline: American Exploration sees '97 production up.

text.p: American Exploration Co said its annual production was rising steadily, with about 124 new wells due to be drilled in 1997 providing exposure to a potential unrisked total 380 billion cubic foot equivalents.
"Production has been moving up at a nice rate and we are hopeful that trend will continue," Chairman and Chief Executive Officer Mark Andrews told Reuters.
The company said it aimed to produce over 20,000 barrels of oil equivalent per day in 1997, compared with a projected 15,300 BOE per day in 1996 and 13,600 BOE per day in 1995.

The 1996 production data was slightly misleading, T. Frank Murphy, vice president of corporate finance, said, because of lower production levels in the first quarter 1996. "We are currently producing over 17,000 BOEs per day," he said.
In 1995, American Exploration drilled 50 new wells and in 1996, it said it expected to drill about 80 new wells.
Andrews and Murphy also said the company was comfortable with analyst consensus cash flow estimates of over $50 million or $3.50 per share in 1997.
Its targeted 1996 operating cash flow was $37 million or between $2.95 and $2.97 per share, versus $27.5 million ot $2.33 per share in 1995, they said.
"The result of rising production and decreasing costs has been really dramatically growing cash flow," Andrews said.
This cash flow stream would fund new wells and projects, the company said.

"Plus, we're going to sell some things that don't fit in our areas, and that will raise some cash to be deployed," Andrews said, citing properties in the Rocky Mountains and some parts of Oklahoma, Mississippi, Alabama and New Mexico.

For the next year, Murphy and Andrews told Reuters the company's projects offshore Texas in state waters offered the most oil and natural gas exposure, followed closely by its Yoakum Gorge project in South Texas.
American Exploration said its strategy for the offshore Texas region was to focus on the so-called state waters, which stretched out for three miles from the beach.
It planned to spend about $46 million in that area in 1997, versus a forecast $35 million in 1996, Andrews said.
Because the shelf area off that coast is already well-developed, many companies are moving into deeper waters.
